title: 360Brew: LLM-based Personalized Ranking and Recommendation - Hamed and Maziar, LinkedIn AI
talk_summary: LinkedIn describes building a single 150B-parameter LLM ('360Brew') that handles many recommendation/ranking tasks via promptification of user history, then distilling it down to a ~3B production model through gradual pruning, distillation, and mixed-precision quantization. The transferable parts are their automation-first experimentation pipeline and their 'go big then go small' distillation recipe, not the recommender specifics.

takeaways.technique: Automated experiment harness that writes results into a shared sheet
takeaways.what_they_do: Every experiment (quantization, pruning, etc.) runs end-to-end from a parameter change and pushes results automatically into a spreadsheet, so developers iterate by clicking rather than wiring pipelines.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the result of the experimental being pushed automatically into the Excel sheet ... automation is the key if you want to basically really optimize

takeaways.technique: Go big then go small (distill from a strong model)
takeaways.what_they_do: They train a large teacher first because small models trained from scratch lack capacity, then distill stepwise (150B -> 8B -> 3B -> 1B) rather than jumping straight to the smallest.
takeaways.evidence_quote: You have to first go big and then go small. If you do try to train the model from scratch with a small model, it doesn't actually work that well.
takeaways.numbers: 150B teacher distilled stepwise to 3B/1B; stepwise distillation 'much much much more effective' than direct 150B->1B

takeaways.technique: Chronological history beats fancy retrieval for recency-biased tasks
takeaways.what_they_do: They tried RAG-style nearest-item retrieval and weighted recency, but found plain chronological ordering was good enough and also avoids breaking KV cache during serving.
takeaways.evidence_quote: for majority of application that we have actually chronical order is good enough ... recommendation systems are very biased to the freshness

takeaways.technique: Mixed-precision: keep the output/scoring head high precision
takeaways.what_they_do: They quantize most layers to FP8 but keep the final LM head in FP32 because lower precision collapses the output distribution and destroys ranking calibration.
takeaways.evidence_quote: in the LM head at the end of the language model has to be in FP32 ... the numbers collapse and you don't have a very good calibration
takeaways.numbers: FP8 elsewhere; FP32 head required to preserve calibration

takeaways.technique: Large held-out benchmark suite incl. out-of-domain tasks to prove generalization
takeaways.what_they_do: They maintain 50-60 benchmarks, some internal some external, including tasks never in training, to verify the model still generalizes and follows instructions.
takeaways.evidence_quote: having a very comprehensive benchmarking set. We have something around like 50 to 60 benchmarking ... some of the tasks are not never being part of our training data
